canonical_question: Does 'grain-boundary-controlled plastic deformation' refer to Coble creep, grain rotation, or boundary sliding as the dominant mechanism?

question_variants.question: Does 'grain-boundary-controlled plastic deformation' refer to Coble creep, grain rotation, or boundary sliding as the dominant mechanism?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The text mentions 'grain-boundary-controlled plastic deformation' in the context of nanocrystalline grains but does not explicitly identify whether the dominant mechanism is Coble creep, grain rotation, or boundary sliding. It attributes high strength to grain boundary strengthening but does not resolve the specific deformation mode.

answers.answer: The evidence mentions 'nanocrystalline grain size and grain-boundary-controlled plastic deformation' but does not specify if the dominant mechanism is Coble creep, grain rotation, or boundary sliding. It infers that solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening cause high compressive strength.
answers.measurement_outcome: nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film, measured compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa
answers.mechanism: solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening
answers.boundary_limitation: Specific deformation mode (Coble creep vs. rotation vs. sliding) is not identified in the text.
evidence_spans: In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering.
A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering.
The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm.
